entries.2663e1e2d95f5a93899ef5afbc34acd1203c0780: <div sID="gen32409" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="4" osisID="1Tim.4" sID="1Tim.4"/> <div eID="gen32409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32410" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen32411" type="x-p"/> Paul here foretels, I. A dreadful apostasy, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. He treats of Christian liberty, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4-1Tim.4.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. He gives Timothy divers directions with respect to himself, his doctrine, and the people under his care, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.6-1Tim.4.16">ver. 6, to the end</reference>.
entries.0dc2c2f445726ace3b5dd908261bd3b558401039: <div eID="gen32411" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen32410" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Apostasy Foretold; Christian Liberty. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32412" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith, giving heed to seducing spirits, and doctrines of devils; <hi type="super">2</hi> Speaking lies in hypocrisy; having their conscience seared with a hot iron; 3 Forbidding to marry, <hi type="italic">and commanding</hi> to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth. <hi type="super">4</hi> For every creature of God <hi type="italic">is</hi> good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving: <hi type="super">5</hi> For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer. <div eID="gen32412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32413" type="x-p"/> We have here a prophecy of the apostasy of the latter times, which he had spoken of as a thing expected and taken for granted among Christians, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.1-2Thess.2.17">2 Thess. ii</reference>. <div eID="gen32413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32414" type="x-p"/> I. In the close of the foregoing chapter, we had the mystery of godliness summed up; and therefore very fitly, in the beginning of this chapter, we have the mystery of iniquity summed up: <hi type="italic">The Spirit speaks expressly that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith;</hi> whether he means the Spirit in the Old Testament, or the Spirit in the prophets of the New Testament, or both. The prophecies concerning antichrist, as well as the prophecies concerning Christ, came from the Spirit. The Spirit in both spoke expressly of a general apostasy from the faith of Christ and the pure worship of God. This should come in the <hi type="italic">latter times,</hi> during the Christian dispensation, for these are called the latter days; in the following ages of the church, for the mystery of iniquity now began to work. <hi type="italic">Some shall depart from the faith,</hi> or there shall be an apostasy from the faith. Some, not all; for in the worst of times God will have a remnant, according to the election of grace. <hi type="italic">They shall depart from the faith,</hi> the faith delivered to the saints (<reference osisRef="Jude.1.3">Jude 3</reference>), which was delivered at once, the sound doctrine of the gospel. <hi type="italic">Giving heed to seducing spirits,</hi> men who pretended to the Spirit, but were not really guided by the Spirit, <reference osisRef="1John.4.1">1 John iv. 1</reference>. <hi type="italic">Beloved, believe not every spirit,</hi> every one who pretends to the Spirit. Now here observe, <div eID="gen32414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32415" type="x-p"/> 1. One of the great instances of the apostasy, namely, giving heed to doctrines of demons, or concerning demons; that is, those doctrines which teach the worship of saints and angels, as a middle sort of deities, between the immortal God and mortal men, such as the heathen called demons, and worshipped under that notion. Now this plainly agrees to the church of Rome, and it was one of the first steps towards that great apostasy, the enshrining of the relics of martyrs, paying divine honours to them, erecting altars, burning incense, consecrating images and temples, and making prayers and praises to the honour of saints departed. This demon-worship is paganism revived, the image of the first beast. <div eID="gen32415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32416" type="x-p"/> 2. The instruments of promoting and propagating this apostasy and delusion. (1.) It will be done by hypocrisy of those that speak lies, the agents and emissaries of Satan, who promote these delusions by lies and forgeries and pretended miracles, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.2">v. 2</reference>. It is done by their hypocrisy, professing honour to Christ, and yet at the same time fighting against all his anointed offices, and corrupting or profaning all his ordinances. This respects also the hypocrisy of those who have <hi type="italic">their consciences seared with a red-hot iron,</hi> who are perfectly lost to the very first principles of virtue and moral honesty. If men had not their consciences seared as with a hot iron, they could never maintain a power to dispense with oaths for the good of the catholic cause, could never maintain that no faith is to be kept with heretics, could never divest themselves of all remains of humanity and compassion, and clothe themselves with the most barbarous cruelty, under pretence of promoting the interest of the church. (2.) Another part of their character is that they forbid to marry, forbid their clergy to marry, and speak very reproachfully of marriage, though an ordinance of God; and that they command <hi type="italic">to abstain from meats,</hi> and place religion in such abstinence at certain times and seasons, only to exercise a tyranny over the consciences of men. <div eID="gen32416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32417" type="x-p"/> 3. On the whole observe, (1.) The apostasy of the latter times should not surprise us, because it was expressly foretold by the Spirit. (2.) The Spirit is God, otherwise he could not certainly foresee such distant events, which as to us are uncertain and contingent, depending on the tempers, humours, and lusts of men. (3.) The difference between the predictions of the Spirit and the oracles of the heathen is remarkable; the Spirit speaks expressly, but the oracles of the heathen were always doubtful and uncertain. (4.) It is comfortable to think that in such general apostasies all are not carried away, but only some. (5.) It is common for seducers and deceivers to pretend to the Spirit, which is a strong presumption that all are convinced that this is the most likely to work in us an approbation of what pretends to come from the Spirit. (6.) Men must be hardened, and their consciences seared, before they can depart from the faith, and draw in others to side with them. (7.) It is a sign that men have departed from the faith when they will command what God has forbidden, such as saint and angel or demon-worship; and forbid what God has allowed or commanded, such as marriage and meats. <div eID="gen32417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32418" type="x-p"/> II. Having mentioned their hypocritical fastings, the apostle takes occasion to lay down the doctrine of the Christian liberty, which we enjoy under the gospel, of using God's good creatures,—that, whereas under the law there was a distinction of meats between clean and unclean (such sorts of flesh they might eat, and such they might not eat), all this is now taken away; and we are to call nothing common or unclean, <reference osisRef="Acts.10.15">Acts x. 15</reference>. Here observe, 1. We are to look upon our food as that which God has created; we have it from him, and therefore must use it for him. 2. God, in making those things, had a special regard to <hi type="italic">those who believe and know the truth,</hi> to good Christians, who have a covenant right to the creatures, whereas others have only a common right. 3. What God has created is to be <hi type="italic">received with thanksgiving.</hi> We must not refuse the gifts of God's bounty, nor be scrupulous in making differences where God has made none; but receive them, and be thankful, acknowledging the power of God the Maker of them, and the bounty of God the giver of them: <hi type="italic">Every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4">v. 4</reference>. This plainly sets us at liberty from all the distinctions of meats appointed by the ceremonial law, as particularly that of swine's flesh, which the Jews were forbidden to eat, but which is allowed to us Christians, by this rule, <hi type="italic">Every creature of God is good,</hi> &c. Observe, God's good creatures are then good, and doubly sweet to us, when they are received with thanksgiving.—<hi type="italic">For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.5">v. 5</reference>. It is a desirable thing to have a sanctified use of our creature-comforts. Now they are sanctified to us, (1.) By the word of God; not only his permission, allowing us the liberty of the use of these things, but his promise to feed us with food convenient for us. This gives us a sanctified use of our creature-comforts. (2.) By prayer, which blesses our meat to us. The word of God and prayer must be brought to our common actions and affairs, and then we do all in faith. Here observe, [1.] Every creature is God's, for he made all. <hi type="italic">Every beast in the forest is mine</hi> (says God), <hi type="italic">and the cattle upon a thousand hills. I know all the fowls of the mountains, and the wild beasts of the field are mine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.50.10-Ps.50.11">Ps. l. 10, 11</reference>. [2.] Every creature of God is good: when the blessed God took a survey of all his works, God saw all that was made, and, behold, it was very good, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.31">Gen. i. 31</reference>. [3.] The blessing of God makes every creature nourishing to us; man lives not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of God (<reference osisRef="Matt.4.4">Matt. iv. 4</reference>), and therefore nothing ought to be refused. [4.] We ought therefore to ask his blessing by prayer, and so to sanctify the creatures we receive by prayer.
entries.bc7d349018a0b73dfc0d47aa7aad70b4bb065a92: <div eID="gen32418" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Exhortation to Godliness; Exhortation to Ministerial Duties. (<hi type="small-caps">a. d.</hi> 64.)</title> <div sID="gen32419" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things, thou shalt be a good minister of Jesus Christ, nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained. <hi type="super">7</hi> But refuse profane and old wives' fables, and exercise thyself <hi type="italic">rather</hi> unto godliness. <hi type="super">8</hi> For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come. <hi type="super">9</hi> This <hi type="italic">is</hi> a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation. <hi type="super">10</hi> For therefore we both labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe. <hi type="super">11</hi> These things command and teach. <hi type="super">12</hi> Let no man despise thy youth; but be thou an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity. <hi type="super">13</hi> Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. <hi type="super">14</hi> Neglect not the gift that is in thee, which was given thee by prophecy, with the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. <hi type="super">15</hi> Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all. <hi type="super">16</hi> Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee. <div eID="gen32419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32420" type="x-p"/> The apostle would have Timothy to instil into the minds of Christians such sentiments as might prevent their being seduced by the judaizing teachers. Observe, Those are good ministers of Jesus Christ who are diligent in their work; not that study to advance new notions, but that <hi type="italic">put the brethren in remembrance of those things which they have received and heard. Wherefore I will not be negligent to put you always in remembrance of these things, though you knew them,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.12">2 Pet. i. 12</reference>. And elsewhere, <hi type="italic">I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.1">2 Pet. iii. 1</reference>. And, says the apostle Jude, <hi type="italic">I will therefore put you in remembrance,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.5">Jude 5</reference>. You see that the apostles and apostolical men reckoned it a main part of their work to put their hearers in remembrance; for we are apt to forget, and slow to learn and remember, the things of God.—<hi type="italic">Nourished up in the words of faith and good doctrine, whereunto thou hast attained.</hi> Observe, 1. Even ministers themselves have need to be growing and increasing in the knowledge of Christ and his doctrine: they must be nourished up in the words of faith. 2. The best way for ministers to grow in knowledge and faith is to put the brethren in remembrance; while we teach others, we teach ourselves. 3. Those whom ministers teach are brethren, and are to be treated like brethren; for ministers are not lords of God's heritage. <div eID="gen32420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32421" type="x-p"/> I. Godliness is here pressed upon him and others: <hi type="italic">Refuse profane and old wives' sayings,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7-1Tim.4.8">v. 7, 8</reference>, The Jewish traditions, which some people fill their heads with, have nothing to do with them. <hi type="italic">But exercise thyself rather unto godliness;</hi> that is, mind practical religion. Those who would be godly must exercise themselves unto godliness; it requires a constant exercise. The reason is taken from the fain of godliness; <hi type="italic">bodily exercise profits little,</hi> or for a little time. Abstinence from meats and marriage, and the like, though they pass for acts of mortification and self-denial, yet profit little, they turn to little account. What will it avail us to mortify the body if we do not mortify sin? Observe, 1. There is a great deal to be got by godliness; it will be of use to us in the whole of our life, for it has <hi type="italic">the promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.</hi> 2. The gain of godliness lies much in the promise: and the promises made to godly people relate to the life that now is, but especially they relate to the life that is to come. Under the Old Testament the promises were mostly of temporal blessings, but under the New Testament of spiritual and eternal blessings. If godly people have but little of the good things of the life that now is, yet it shall be made up to them in the good things of the life that is to come. 3. There were profane and old wives' fables in the days of the apostles; and Timothy, though an excellent man, was not above such a word of advice, <hi type="italic">Refuse profane,</hi> &c. 4. It is not enough that we refuse profane and old wives' fables, but we must exercise ourselves to godliness; we must not only cease to do evil, but we must learn to do well (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.16-Isa.1.17">Isa. i. 16, 17</reference>), and we must make a practice of exercising ourselves to godliness. And, 5. Those who are truly godly shall not be losers at last, whatever becomes of those who content themselves with bodily exercise, for godliness has the promise, &c. <div eID="gen32421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32422" type="x-p"/> II. The encouragement which we have to proceed in the ways of godliness, and to exercise ourselves to it, notwithstanding the difficulties and discouragements that we meet with in it. He had said (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">v. 8</reference>) that it <hi type="italic">is profitable for all things, having the promise of the life which now is.</hi> But the question is, Will the profit balance the loss? For, if it will not, it is not profit. Yes, we are sure it will. Here is another of Paul's faithful sayings, worthy of all acceptation—that all our labours and losses in the service of God and the work of religion will be abundantly recompensed, so that though we lose for Christ we shall not lose by him. <hi type="italic">Therefore we labour and suffer reproach, because we trust in the living God,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">v. 10</reference>. Observe, <div eID="gen32422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32423" type="x-p"/> 1. Godly people must labour and expect reproach; they must do well, and yet expect at the same time to suffer ill: toil and trouble are to be expected by us in this world, not only as men, but as saints. <div eID="gen32423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32424" type="x-p"/> 2. Those who labour and suffer reproach in the service of God and the work of religion may depend upon the living God that they shall not lose by it. Let this encourage them, <hi type="italic">We trust in the living God.</hi> The consideration of this, that the God who has undertaken to be our pay-master is the living God, who does himself live for ever and is the fountain of life to all who serve him, should encourage us in all our services and in all our sufferings for him, especially considering that he is <hi type="italic">the Saviour of all men.</hi> (1.) By his providences he protects the persons, and prolongs the lives, of the children of men. (2.) He has a general good-will to the eternal salvation of all men thus far that he is not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance. He desires not the death of sinners; he is thus far the Saviour of all men that none are left in the same desperate condition that fallen angels are in. Now, if he be thus the Saviour of all men, we may hence infer that much more he will be the rewarder of those who seek and serve him; if he has such a good-will for all his creatures, much more will he provide well for those who are new creatures, who are born again. He is the Saviour of all men, but <hi type="italic">especially of those that believe;</hi> and the salvation he has in store for those that believe is sufficient to recompense them for all their services and sufferings. Here we see, [1.] The life of a Christian is a life of labour and suffering: <hi type="italic">We labour and suffer.</hi> [2.] The best we can expect to suffer in the present life is reproach for our well-doing, for our work of faith and labour of love. [3.] True Christians trust in the living God; for cursed is the man that trusts in man, or in any but the living God; and those that trust in him shall never be ashamed. <hi type="italic">Trust in him at all times.</hi> [4.] God is the general Saviour of all men, as he has put them into a salvable state; but he is in a particular manner the Saviour of true believers; there is then a general and a special redemption. <div eID="gen32424" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32425" type="x-p"/> III. He concludes the chapter with an exhortation to Timothy, <div eID="gen32425" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32426" type="x-p"/> 1. To <hi type="italic">command and teach these things</hi> that he had now been teaching him. "Command them to exercise themselves unto godliness, teach them the profit of it, and that if they serve God they serve one who will be sure to bear them out." <div eID="gen32426" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32427" type="x-p"/> 2. To conduct himself with that gravity and prudence which might gain him respect, notwithstanding his youth: "<hi type="italic">Let no man despise thy youth;</hi> that is, give no man an occasion to despise thy youth." Men's youth will not be despised if they do not by youthful vanities and follies make themselves despicable; and this men may do who are old, who may therefore thank themselves if they be despised. <div eID="gen32427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32428" type="x-p"/> 3. To confirm his doctrine by a good example: <hi type="italic">Be thou an example of the believers,</hi> &c. Observe, Those who teach by their doctrine must teach by their live, else they pull down with one hand what they build up with the other: they must be examples both <hi type="italic">in word and conversation.</hi> Their discourse must be edifying, and this will be a good example: their conversation must be strict, and this will be a good example: they must be examples <hi type="italic">in charity,</hi> or love to God and all good men, examples <hi type="italic">in spirit,</hi> that is, in spiritual-mindedness, in spiritual worship,—<hi type="italic">in faith,</hi> that is, in the profession of Christian faith,—and <hi type="italic">in purity</hi> or chastity. <div eID="gen32428" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32429" type="x-p"/> 4. He charges him to study hard: <hi type="italic">Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine, to meditation upon these things,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.13">v. 13</reference>. Though Timothy had extraordinary gifts, yet he must use ordinary means. Or it may be meant of the public reading of the scriptures; he must <hi type="italic">read and exhort,</hi> that is, read and expound, read and press what he read upon them; he must expound it both by way of exhortation and by way of doctrine; he must teach them both what to do and what to believe. Observe, (1.) Ministers must teach and command the things that they are themselves taught and commanded to do; they must teach people to observe all things whatsoever Christ has commanded, <reference osisRef="Matt.28.20">Matt. xxviii. 20</reference>. (2.) The best way for ministers to avoid being despised is to teach and practise the things that are given them in charge. No wonder if ministers are despised who do not teach these things, or who, instead of being examples of good to believers, act directly contrary to the doctrines they preach; for ministers are to be ensamples of their flock. (3.) Those ministers that are the best accomplished for their work must yet mind their studies, that they may be improving in knowledge; and they must mind also their work; they are to give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. <div eID="gen32429" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32430" type="x-p"/> 5. He charges him to beware of negligence: <hi type="italic">Neglect not the gift that is in thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">v. 14</reference>. The gifts of God will wither if they be neglected. It may be understood either of the office to which he was advanced, or of his qualifications for that office; if of the former, it was ordination in an ordinary way; if of the latter, it was extraordinary. It seems to be the former, for it was by <hi type="italic">laying on of hands,</hi> &c. Here see the scripture-way of ordination: it was by the laying on of hands, and the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. Observe, Timothy was ordained by men in office. It was an extraordinary gift that we read of elsewhere as being conferred on him by the laying on of Paul's hands, but he was invested in the office of the ministry by the laying on of the hands of the presbytery. (1.) We may note, The office of the ministry is a gift, it is the gift of Christ; when he ascended on high, he received gifts for men, and he gave some apostles, and some pastors and teachers (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Eph. iv. 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">11</reference>), and this was a very kind gift to his church. (2.) Ministers ought not to neglect the gift bestowed upon them, whether by gift we are here to understand the office of the ministry or the qualifications for the office; neither the one nor the other must be neglected. (3.) Though there was a prophecy in the case of Timothy (the gift was given by prophecy), yet this was accompanied by the laying on of the hands of the presbytery, that is, a number of presbyters; the office was conveyed to him this way; and I should think here is a sufficient warrant for ordination by presbyters, since it does not appear that Paul was concerned in Timothy's ordination. It is true, extraordinary gifts were conferred on him by the laying on of the apostle's hands (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2 Tim. i. 6</reference>), but, if he was concerned in his ordination, the presbytery was not excluded, for that is particularly mentioned, whence it seems pretty evident that the presbytery have the inherent power of ordination. <div eID="gen32430" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32431" type="x-p"/> 6. Having this work committed to him, he must <hi type="italic">give himself wholly</hi> to it: "Be wholly in those things, <hi type="italic">that thy profiting may appear.</hi>" He was a wise knowing man, and yet must still be profiting, and make it appear that he improved in knowledge. Observe, (1.) Ministers are to be much in meditation. They are to consider beforehand how and what they must speak. They are to meditate on the great trust committed to them, on the worth and value of immortal souls, and on the account they must give at the last. (2.) Ministers must be wholly in these things, they must mind these things as their principal work and business: <hi type="italic">Give thyself wholly to them.</hi> (3.) By this means their profiting will appear in all things, as well a to all persons; this is the way for them to profit in knowledge and grace, and also to profit others. <div eID="gen32431" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen32432" type="x-p"/> 7. He presses it upon him to be very cautious: "<hi type="italic">Take heed to thyself and to the doctrine,</hi> consider what thou preachest; <hi type="italic">continue in them,</hi> in the truths that thou hast received; and this will be the way to <hi type="italic">save thyself, and those that hear thee.</hi>" Observe, (1.) Ministers are engaged in saving work, which makes it a good work. (2.) The care of ministers should be in the first place to save themselves: "Save thyself in the first place, so shalt thou be instrumental to save those that hear thee." (3.) Ministers in preaching should aim at the salvation of those that hear them, next to the salvation of their own souls. (4.) The best way to answer both these ends is to take heed to ourselves, &c.  <chapter eID="1Tim.4"/> <div eID="gen32432" type="x-p"/>

entries.e4d4ab3301a15368edd267617b43c79faed8ea0f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18107"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 4</title> <div sID="gen37273" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.16">1Ti 4:1-16</reference>. Prediction of a Coming Departure from the Faith: Timothy's Duty as to It: General Directions to Him.<div eID="gen37273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37274" type="x-p"/> The "mystery of iniquity" here alluded to, and already working (<reference osisRef="2Thess.2.7">2Th 2:7</reference>), stands opposed to the "mystery of godliness" just mentioned (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.16">1Ti 3:16</reference>).<div eID="gen37274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37275" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18107"/><hi type="bold">1. Now--</hi>Greek, "But." In contrast to the "mystery of godliness."<div eID="gen37275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37276" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Spirit--</hi>speaking by the prophets in the Church (whose prophecies rested on those of the Old Testament, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.25">Da 7:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.8.23">8:23</reference>, &c.; 11:30, as also on those of Jesus in the New Testament, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.11-Matt.24.24">Mt 24:11-24</reference>), and also by Paul himself, <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2Th 2:3</reference> (with whom accord <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.3">2Pe 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.2.18">1Jo 2:18</reference>; Jude 18).<div eID="gen37276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37277" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">expressly--</hi>"in plain words." This shows that he refers to prophecies of the Spirit then lying before him.<div eID="gen37277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37278" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the latter times--</hi>in the times following upon the times in which he is now writing. Not some remote future, but times immediately subsequent, the beginnings of the apostasy being already discernible (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.29">Ac 20:29</reference>): these are the forerunners of "the last days" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.1">2Ti 3:1</reference>).<div eID="gen37278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37279" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">depart from the faith--</hi>The apostasy was to be within the Church, the faithful one becoming the harlot. In <reference osisRef="2Thess.2.3">2Th 2:3</reference> (written earlier), the apostasy of the Jews from God (joining the heathen against Christianity) is the groundwork on which the prophecy rises; whereas here, in the Pastoral Epistles, the prophecy is connected with Gnostic errors, the seeds of which had already been sown in the Church [Auberlen] (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>). Apollonius Tyanæus, a heretic, came to Ephesus in the lifetime of Timothy.<div eID="gen37279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37280" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">giving heed--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37281" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">seducing spirits--</hi>working in the heretical teachers. <reference osisRef="1John.4.2">1Jo 4:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1John.3.6">3, 6</reference>, "the spirit of error," opposed to "the spirit of truth," "the Spirit" which "speaketh" in the true prophets against them.<div eID="gen37281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37282" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrines of devils--</hi>literally "teachings of (that is suggested by) demons." <reference osisRef="Jas.3.15">Jas 3:15</reference>, "wisdom ... devilish"; <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.15">2Co 11:15</reference>, "Satan's ministers." <div eID="gen37282" type="x-p"/>
entries.22f546f4e65e3d9585c17ebc031b125dd925b5d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18108"/><div sID="gen37283" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18108"/>2. Rather translate, "Through (literally, 'in'; the element in which the apostasy has place) the hypocrisy of lying speakers"; this expresses the means through which "some shall (be led to) depart from the faith," namely, the reigned sanctity of the seducers (compare "deceivers," <reference osisRef="Titus.1.10">Tit 1:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37284" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having their conscience seared--</hi>Greek, "having their own conscience," &c., that is, not only "speaking lies" to others, but also having their own conscience seared. Professing to lead others to holiness, their own conscience is all the while defiled. Bad consciences always have recourse to hypocrisy. As faith and a good conscience are joined (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.5">1Ti 1:5</reference>); so hypocrisy (that is, unbelief, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.5">Mt 24:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.51">51</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Luke.12.46">Lu 12:46</reference>) and a bad conscience here. Theodoret explains like English Version, "seared," as implying their extreme insensibility; the effect of cauterizing being to deaden sensation. The Greek, however, primarily means "branded" with the consciousness of crimes committed against their better knowledge and conscience, like so many scars burnt in by a branding iron: Compare <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.11">3:11</reference>, "condemned of himself." They are conscious of the brand within, and yet with a hypocritical show of sanctity, they strive to seduce others. As "a seal" is used in a good sense (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.19">2Ti 2:19</reference>), so "a brand" in a bad sense. The image is taken from the branding of criminals. <div eID="gen37284" type="x-p"/>
entries.d0699934ab9762c89a2a14ccf824fd4d63e6baf3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18109"/><div sID="gen37285" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18109"/>3. Sensuality leads to false spiritualism. Their own inward impurity is reflected in their eyes in the world without them, and hence their asceticism (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.15">15</reference>) [Wiesinger]. By a spurious spiritualism (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.18">2Ti 2:18</reference>), which made moral perfection consist in abstinence from outward things, they pretended to attain to a higher perfection. <reference osisRef="Matt.19.10-Matt.19.12">Mt 19:10-12</reference> (compare <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.8">1Co 7:8</reference>, 26, 38) gave a seeming handle to their "forbidding marriage" (contrast <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.14">1Ti 5:14</reference>); and the Old Testament distinction as to clean and unclean, gave a pretext for teaching to "abstain from meats" (compare <reference osisRef="Col.2.16">Col 2:16</reference>, 17, 20-23). As these Judaizing Gnostics combined the harlot or apostate Old Testament Church with the beast (<reference osisRef="Rev.17.3">Re 17:3</reference>), or Gnostic spiritualizing anti-Christianity, so Rome's Judaizing elements (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>) shall ultimately be combined with the open worldly-wise anti-Christianity of the false prophet or beast (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.21">21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.2.8">Col 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.1-1John.4.3">1Jo 4:1-3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.13.12-Rev.13.15">Re 13:12-15</reference>). Austerity gained for them a show of sanctity while preaching false doctrine (<reference osisRef="Col.2.23">Col 2:23</reference>). Eusebius [Ecclesiastical History, 4.29] quotes from Irenæus [1.28] a statement that Saturninus, Marcion, and the Encratites preached abstinence from marriage and animal meats. Paul prophetically warns against such notions, the seeds of which already were being sown (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1Ti 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>, 18).<div eID="gen37285" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37286" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to be received--</hi>Greek, "to be partaken of."<div eID="gen37286" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37287" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of them--</hi>literally, (created and designed) "for them," Though all (even the unbelieving, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.14">Psa 104:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mt 5:45</reference>) are partakers in these foods created by God, "they which believe" alone fulfil God's design in creation by partaking of them with thanksgiving; as opposed to those who abstain from them, or in partaking of them, do not do so with thanksgiving. The unbelieving have not the designed use of such foods by reason of their "conscience being defiled" (<reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>). The children of God alone "inherit the earth"; for obedience is the necessary qualification (as it was in the original grant of the earth to Adam), which they alone possess.<div eID="gen37287" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37288" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and know the truth--</hi>explanatory and defining who are "they which believe." Translate as Greek, "and have full knowledge of the truth" (see on <reference osisRef="Phil.1.9">Php 1:9</reference>). Thus he contradicts the assumption of superior knowledge and higher moral perfection, put forward by the heretics, on the ground of their abstinence from marriage and meats. "The truth" stands in opposition to their "lies" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.2">1Ti 4:2</reference>). <div eID="gen37288" type="x-p"/>
entries.671632e0455f15ed0eedbe00b04df4e3ce26cac2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18110"/><div sID="gen37289" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18110"/><hi type="bold">4-5. Translate as Greek, "Because" (expressing a reason resting on an objective fact; or, as here, a Scripture quotation)--</hi>"For" (a reason resting on something subjective in the writer's mind).<div eID="gen37289" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37290" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">every creature ... good--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Gen.1.31">Ge 1:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.14.14">Ro 14:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.14.20">20</reference>). A refutation by anticipation of the Gnostic opposition to creation: the seeds of which were now lurking latently in the Church. Judaism (<reference osisRef="Acts.10.11-Acts.10.16">Ac 10:11-16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.25">1Co 10:25</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.10.26">26</reference>) was the starting-point of the error as to meats: Oriental Gnosis added new elements. The old Gnostic heresy is now almost extinct; but its remains in the celibacy of Rome's priesthood, and in its fasts from animal meats, enjoined under the penalty of mortal sin, remain.<div eID="gen37290" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37291" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">if ... with thanksgiving--</hi>Meats, though pure in themselves, become impure by being received with an unthankful mind (<reference osisRef="Rom.14.6">Ro 14:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.15">Tit 1:15</reference>). <div eID="gen37291" type="x-p"/>
entries.2ecff3ad81d9763d854b432bfce94759bd547fb6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18112"/><div sID="gen37294" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18112"/><hi type="bold">6. If thou put ... in remembrance--</hi>rather as Greek, "If thou suggest to (bring under the notice of) the brethren," &c.<div eID="gen37294" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37295" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these things--</hi>namely, the truths stated in <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.4">1Ti 4:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.5">5</reference>, in opposition to the errors foretold, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:1-3</reference>.<div eID="gen37295" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37296" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">minister--</hi>"servant."<div eID="gen37296" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37297" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">nourished up--</hi>The Greek is present, not past: "continually being nourished in" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.5">2Ti 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">3:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.15">15</reference>).<div eID="gen37297" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37298" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the words of faith--</hi>rather, "the words of the faith" (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37298" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37299" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">good doctrine--</hi>"the good teaching." Explanatory of "the faith," in opposition to the "teachings of demons" (English Version, "doctrines of devils," <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1">1Ti 4:1</reference>) which Timothy was to counteract. Compare "sound doctrine" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.10">1Ti 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.3">6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.9">Tit 1:9</reference>; 2:1).<div eID="gen37299" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37300" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whereunto thou hast attained--</hi>"the course of which thou hast followed"; hast followed along by tracing its course and accompanying it [Alford]. Thou hast begun to follow up [Bengel]. The same Greek occurs, "thou hast fully known" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.10">2Ti 3:10</reference>), "having had perfect understanding" (<reference osisRef="Luke.1.3">Lu 1:3</reference>). It is an undesigned coincidence that the Greek verb is used only by Paul and Paul's companion, Luke. <div eID="gen37300" type="x-p"/>
entries.0317157fb785c21c3fbb92ba896f35ea65f4d293: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18113"/><div sID="gen37301" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18113"/><hi type="bold">7. refuse--</hi>reject, avoid, have nothing to do with (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.23">2Ti 2:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.3.10">Tit 3:10</reference>).<div eID="gen37301" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37302" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">old wives' fables--</hi>anile myths (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.4">1Ti 1:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.14">Tit 1:14</reference>). They are "profane," because leading away from "godliness" or "piety" (1Ti 1:4-7; 6:20; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.16">2Ti 2:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.1.1">Tit 1:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.1.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen37302" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37303" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exercise thyself--</hi>literally, "exercise thyself" as one undergoing training in a gymnasium. Let thy self-discipline be not in ascetical exercises as the false teachers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">8</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Ti 2:22</reference>, 23; <reference osisRef="Heb.5.14">He 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.11">12:11</reference>), but with a view to godliness or "piety" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.11">1Ti 6:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.12">12</reference>). <div eID="gen37303" type="x-p"/>
entries.c32a6b07dc69f03840c578e8b09861473e4d6394: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18114"/><div sID="gen37304" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18114"/><hi type="bold">8. profiteth little--</hi>Greek, "profiteth to (but) a small extent." Paul does not deny that fasting and abstinence from conjugal intercourse for a time, with a view to reaching the inward man through the outward, do profit somewhat, <reference osisRef="Acts.13.3">Ac 13:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.5">1Co 7:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.7.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.26">9:26</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.27">27</reference> (though in its degenerate form, asceticism, dwelling solely on what is outward, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.3">1Ti 4:3</reference>, is not only not profitable but injurious). Timothy seems to have had a leaning to such outward self-discipline (compare <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.23">1Ti 5:23</reference>). Paul, therefore, while not disapproving of this in its due proportion and place, shows the vast superiority of godliness or piety, as being profitable not merely "to a small extent," but unto all things; for, having its seat within, it extends thence to the whole outward life of a man. Not unto one portion only of his being, but to every portion of it, bodily and spiritual, temporal and eternal [Alford]. "He who has piety (which is 'profitable unto all things') wants nothing needed to his well-being, even though he be without those helps which, 'to a small extent,' bodily exercise furnishes" [Calvin]. "Piety," which is the end for which thou art to "exercise thyself" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">1Ti 4:7</reference>), is the essential thing: the means are secondary.<div eID="gen37304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37305" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having promise, &c.--</hi>Translate as Greek, "Having promise of life, that which now is, and that which is to come." "Life" in its truest and best sense now and hereafter (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.1">2Ti 1:1</reference>). Length of life now so far as it is really good for the believer; life in its truest enjoyments and employments now, and life blessed and eternal hereafter (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.33">Mt 6:33</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.10.29">Mr 10:29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Mark.10.30">30</reference>). "Now in this time" (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.11">Psa 84:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.112.1-Ps.112.10">112:1-10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.8.28">Ro 8:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.21">1Co 3:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.22">22</reference>, "all things are yours ... the world, life ... things present, things to come"). Christianity, which seems to aim only at our happiness hereafter, effectually promotes it here (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.6">1Ti 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.1.3">2Pe 1:3</reference>). Compare Solomon's prayer and the answer (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.3.7-1Kgs.3.13">1Ki 3:7-13</reference>). <div eID="gen37305" type="x-p"/>
entries.23ed6dde424da7ff7c0ec2d604f0a1ef760facd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18115"/><div sID="gen37306" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18115"/>9. (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>). This verse (Greek), "faithful is the saying, " &c. confirms the assertion as to the "promise" attached to "godliness," <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>, and forms a prefatory introduction to <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Ti 4:10</reference>, which is joined to <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.9">1Ti 4:9</reference> by "For." So <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.11">2Ti 2:11</reference>. Godly men seem to suffer loss as to this life: Paul hereby refutes the notion [Bengel]. "God is the Saviour specially of those that believe" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Ti 4:10</reference>), both as to "the life that now is," and also as to "the life which is to come" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>). <div eID="gen37306" type="x-p"/>
entries.646a8bc12ad378d7531a9eea1fec8eacf5b34168: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18116"/><div sID="gen37307" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18116"/><hi type="bold">10. therefore--</hi>Greek, "with a view to this." The reason why "we both ('both' is omitted in the oldest manuscripts) labor (endure hardship) and suffer reproach (some oldest manuscripts read 'strive') is because we have rested, and do rest our hope, on the living (and therefore, life-giving, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>) God."<div eID="gen37307" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37308" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Saviour--</hi>even in this life (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:8</reference>).<div eID="gen37308" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37309" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">specially of those that believe--</hi>Their "labor and reproach" are not inconsistent with their having from the living God, their Saviour, even the present life (<reference osisRef="Mark.10.30">Mr 10:30</reference>, "a hundred fold now in this time ... with persecutions"), much more the life to come. If God is in a sense "Saviour" of unbelievers (<reference osisRef="1Tim.2.4">1Ti 2:4</reference>, that is, is willing to be so everlastingly, and is temporally here their Preserver and Benefactor), much more of believers. He is the Saviour of all men potentially (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Ti 1:15</reference>); of believers alone effectually. <div eID="gen37309" type="x-p"/>
entries.330daaf76f27a67e8b3e4b965994b46c33cbd453: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18117"/><div sID="gen37310" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18117"/>11. These truths, to the exclusion of those useless and even injurious teachings (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.8">1Ti 4:1-8</reference>), while weighing well thyself, charge also upon others. <div eID="gen37310" type="x-p"/>
entries.657bed7e2f464cae5da946b541922cc1b7b38360: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18118"/><div sID="gen37311" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18118"/><hi type="bold">12. Let no man despise thy youth--</hi>Act so as to be respected in spite of thy youth (<reference osisRef="1Cor.16.11">1Co 16:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.15">Tit 2:15</reference>); compare "youthful" as to Timothy (<reference osisRef="2Tim.2.22">2Ti 2:22</reference>). He was but a mere youth when he joined Paul (<reference osisRef="Acts.16.1-Acts.16.3">Ac 16:1-3</reference>). Eleven years had elapsed since then to the time subsequent to Paul's first imprisonment. He was, therefore, still young; especially in comparison with Paul, whose place he was filling; also in relation to elderly presbyters whom he should "entreat as a father" (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.1">1Ti 5:1</reference>), and generally in respect to his duties in rebuking, exhorting, and ordaining (<reference osisRef="1Tim.3.1">1Ti 3:1</reference>), which ordinarily accord best with an elderly person (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.19">1Ti 5:19</reference>).<div eID="gen37311" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37312" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">be thou an example--</hi>Greek, "become a pattern" (<reference osisRef="Titus.2.7">Tit 2:7</reference>); the true way of making men not to despise (slight, or disregard) thy youth.<div eID="gen37312" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37313" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in word--</hi>in all that thou sayest in public and private.<div eID="gen37313" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37314" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">conversation--</hi>that is, "behavior" the Old English sense of the word.<div eID="gen37314" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37315" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in charity ... faith--</hi>the two cardinal principles of the Christian (<reference osisRef="Gal.5.6">Ga 5:6</reference>). The oldest manuscripts omit, "in spirit."<div eID="gen37315" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37316" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in purity--</hi>simplicity of holy motive followed out in consistency of holy action [Alford] (<reference osisRef="1Tim.5.22">1Ti 5:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.6">2Co 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.3.17">Jas 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.4.8">4:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.22">1Pe 1:22</reference>). <div eID="gen37316" type="x-p"/>
entries.7bcdf4e91f5c823fbaed4a177629b7a6f08a9aba: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18119"/><div sID="gen37317" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18119"/><hi type="bold">13. Till I come--</hi>when Timothy's commission would be superseded for the time by the presence of the apostle himself (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.3">1Ti 1:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.3.14">3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37317" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37318" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reading--</hi>especially in the public congregation. The practice of reading Scripture was transferred from the Jewish synagogue to the Christian Church (<reference osisRef="Luke.4.16-Luke.4.20">Lu 4:16-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.15">Ac 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.15.21">15:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.14">2Co 3:14</reference>). The New Testament Gospel and Epistles being recognized as inspired by those who had the gift of discerning spirits, were from the first, according as they were written, read along with the Old Testament in the Church (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.21">1Th 5:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Col.4.16">Col 4:16</reference>), [Justin Martyr, Apology, 1.67]. I think that while public reading is the prominent thought, the Spirit intended also to teach that Scripture reading in private should be "the fountain of all wisdom from which pastors ought to draw whatever they bring before their flock" [Alford].<div eID="gen37318" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37319" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exhortation--</hi>addressed to the feelings and will with a view to the regulation of the conduct.<div eID="gen37319" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37320" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">doctrine--</hi>Greek (ministerial), "teaching" or instruction. Addressed to the understanding, so as to impart knowledge (<reference osisRef="1Tim.6.2">1Ti 6:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.12.7">Ro 12:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.12.8">8</reference>). Whether in public or private, exhortation and instruction should be based on Scripture reading. <div eID="gen37320" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd644e442a4d69612d550fb34e8291651d6a1fee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18120"/><div sID="gen37321" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18120"/><hi type="bold">14. Neglect not the gift--</hi>by letting it lie unused. In <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference> the gift is represented as a spark of the Spirit lying within him, and sure to smoulder by neglect, the stirring up or keeping in lively exercise of which depends on the will of him on whom it is bestowed (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.18">Mt 25:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.27">25, 27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.28">28</reference>). The charism or spiritual gift, is that of the Spirit which qualified him for "the work of an evangelist" (<reference osisRef="Eph.4.11">Ep 4:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.4.5">2Ti 4:5</reference>), or perhaps the gift of discerning spirits, specially needed in his function of ordaining, as overseer [Bishop Hinds].<div eID="gen37321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37322" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">given thee--</hi>by God (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.4">1Co 12:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.12.6">6</reference>).<div eID="gen37322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37323" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">by prophecy--</hi>that is, by the Holy Spirit, at his general ordination, or else consecration, to the special see of Ephesus, speaking through the prophets God's will to give him the graces needed to qualify him for his work (<reference osisRef="1Tim.1.18">1Ti 1:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.13.1-Acts.13.3">Ac 13:1-3</reference>).<div eID="gen37323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37324" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... laying on of ... hands--</hi>So in Joshua's case (<reference osisRef="Num.27.18-Num.27.20">Nu 27:18-20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.34.9">De 34:9</reference>). The gift was connected with the symbolical act of laying on hands. But the Greek "with" implies that the presbyter's laying on hands was the mere accompaniment of the conferring of the gift. "By" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference>) implies that Paul's laying on his hands was the actual instrument of its being conferred.<div eID="gen37324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37325" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the presbytery--</hi>In <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.6">2Ti 1:6</reference> the apostle mentions only his own laying on of hands. But there his aim is to remind Timothy specially of the part he himself took in imparting to him the gift. Here he mentions the fact, quite consistent with the other, that the neighboring presbyters took part in the ordination or consecration, he, however, taking the foremost part. Paul, though having the general oversight of the elders everywhere, was an elder himself (<reference osisRef="1Pet.5.1">1Pe 5:1</reference>; 2Jo 1). The Jewish council was composed of the elders of the Church (the presbytery, <reference osisRef="Luke.22.66">Lu 22:66</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.22.5">Ac 22:5</reference>), and a presiding rabbi; so the Christian Church was composed of apostles, elders, and a president (<reference osisRef="Acts.15.16">Ac 15:16</reference>). As the president of the synagogue was of the same order as his presbyters, so the bishop was of the same order as his presbyters. At the ordination of the president of the synagogue there were always three presbyters present to lay on hands, so the early Church canons required three bishops to be present at the consecration of a bishop. As the president of the synagogue, so the bishop of the Church alone could ordain, he acting as the representative, and in the name of the whole presbytery [Vitringa]. So, in the Anglican Church, the bishop ordains, the presbyters or priests present joining with him in laying on hands. <div eID="gen37325" type="x-p"/>
entries.c87901653d48fa46546dda6e57c609aba81907c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18121"/><div sID="gen37326" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18121"/><hi type="bold">15. Meditate--</hi>Greek, "Meditate CAREFULLY upon" (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.2">Psa 1:2</reference>; 119:15; compare "Isaac," <reference osisRef="Gen.24.63">Ge 24:63</reference>).<div eID="gen37326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37327" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">these things--</hi>(<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12-1Tim.4.14">1Ti 4:12-14</reference>). As food would not nourish without digestion, which assimilates the food to the substance of the body, so spiritual food, in order to benefit us, needs to be appropriated by prayerful meditation.<div eID="gen37327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37328" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">give thyself wholly to--</hi>literally, "BE in these things"; let them engross thee wholly; be wholly absorbed in them. Entire self-dedication, as in other pursuits, so especially in religion, is the secret of proficiency. There are changes as to all other studies, fashionable to-day, out of fashion to-morrow; this study alone is never obsolete, and when made the all-engrossing aim sanctifies all other studies. The exercise of the ministry threatens the spirit of the ministry, unless it be sustained within. The minister must be first his own scholar before he can be another's teacher.<div eID="gen37328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37329" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">profiting--</hi>Greek, "progress" towards perfection in the Christian life, and especially towards the fullest realization of the ideal of a Christian minister (<reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>).<div eID="gen37329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37330" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">may appear to all--</hi>not for thy glory, but for the winning of souls (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.16">Mt 5:16</reference>). <div eID="gen37330" type="x-p"/>
entries.dae4fd43fb84ad7c89295e231f2c3c331ec26277: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv18122"/><div sID="gen37331" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv18122"/><hi type="bold">16. Take heed--</hi>Give heed (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.5">Ac 3:5</reference>).<div eID="gen37331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37332" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thyself, and ... doctrine--</hi>"and unto thy teaching." The two requisites of a good pastor: His teaching will be of no avail unless his own life accord with it; and his own purity of life is not enough unless he be diligent in teaching [Calvin]. This verse is a summary of <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Ti 4:12</reference>.<div eID="gen37332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37333" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">continue in them--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Tim.3.14">2Ti 3:14</reference>).<div eID="gen37333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37334" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in doing this--</hi>not "by doing this," as though he could save himself by works.<div eID="gen37334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen37335" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thou shalt ... save thyself, and them that hear thee--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.33.9">Eze 33:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.20">Jas 5:20</reference>). In performing faithfully his duty to others, the minister is promoting his own salvation. Indeed he cannot "give heed unto the teaching" of others, unless he be at the same time "giving heed unto himself." <chapter eID="1Tim.4"/>

entries.8c0829b4d9c5fc714cb254f07b65acbf57e6701d: <div eID="gen51705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen51706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen51706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen51708" type="x-p"/> Apostasy from the true faith predicted, and in what that apostasy should consist, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.1-1Tim.4.5">1Tim 4:1-5</reference>. Exhortations to Timothy to teach the truth, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.6">1Tim 4:6</reference>. To avoid old wives' fables; to exercise himself to godliness, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.7">1Tim 4:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.8">1Tim 4:8</reference>. To labor, command, and teach, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.9">1Tim 4:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.10">1Tim 4:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.11">1Tim 4:11</reference>. To act so that none might despise his youth, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.12">1Tim 4:12</reference>. To give attendance to reading and preaching, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.13">1Tim 4:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.14">1Tim 4:14</reference>. To give up himself wholly to the Divine work, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.15">1Tim 4:15</reference>. And so doing he should both save himself and them that heard him, <reference osisRef="1Tim.4.16">1Tim 4:16</reference>. <div eID="gen51708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen51709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51710" type="x-p"/> Now the Spirit speaketh expressly - Ῥητως· Manifestly, openly. It is very likely that the apostle refers here to a prophecy then furnished by the Holy Ghost, and probably immediately after he had written the words in the preceding verses; and as this prophecy contains things nowhere else spoken of in the sacred writings, and of the utmost moment to the Christian Church, we cannot hear or read them with too much reverence or respect. <div eID="gen51710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51711" type="x-p"/> In the latter times - This does not necessarily imply the last ages of the world, but any times consequent to those in which the Church then lived. <div eID="gen51711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51712" type="x-p"/> Depart from the faith - Αποστησονται - της πιστεως· They will apostatize from the faith, i.e. from Christianity; renouncing the whole system in effect, by bringing in doctrines which render its essential truths null and void, or denying and renouncing such doctrines as are essential to Christianity as a system of salvation. A man may hold all the truths of Christianity, and yet render them of none effect by holding other doctrines which counteract their influence; or he may apostatize by denying some essential doctrine, though he bring in nothing heterodox. <div eID="gen51712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51713" type="x-p"/> Giving heed to seducing spirits - Πνευμασι πλανοις· Many MSS. and the chief of the fathers have πνευμασι πλανης· spirits of deceit; which is much more emphatic than the common reading. Deception has her spirits, emissaries of every kind, which she employs to darken the hearts and destroy the souls of men. Pretenders to inspiration, and false teachers of every kind, belong to this class. <div eID="gen51713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51714" type="x-p"/> And doctrines of devils - Δαιμονιων· Demons; either meaning fallen spirits, or dead men, spectres, etc., or doctrines inspired by Satan relative to these, by which he secures his own interest, and provides for his own worship.
entries.e39be7682859378fcd4a487fc0dbfbc4e4e05765: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen51714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51715" type="x-p"/> Speaking lies in hypocrisy - Persons pretending, not only to Divine inspiration, but also to extraordinary degrees of holiness, self-denial, mortification, etc., in order to accredit the lies and false doctrines which they taught. Multitudes of lies were framed concerning miracles wrought by the relics of departed saints, as they were termed. For, even in this country, Thomas a Becket was, deemed a saint, his relics wrought numerous miracles; and his tomb was frequented by multitudes of pilgrims! However, as he works none now, we may rest assured that he never did work any. In 1305, King Edward I. was prevailed on by his clergy to write to Pope Clement V. to canonize Thomas de Cantelupo, bishop of Hereford, because a multitude of miracles had been wrought by his influence; In tantum, says the king, quod ipsius meritis et intercessionibus gloriosis, lumen caecis, surdis auditus, verbum mutis, et gressus claudis, et alia pleraque beneficia ipsius patrocinium implorantibus, caelesti dextra conferuntur. "Insomuch that, by his glorious merits and intercessions, the blind receive their sight, the deaf hear, the dumb speak, and the lame walk; and many other benefits are conferred by the right hand of the Divine Being on those who implore his patronage." And therefore he prays that this dead bishop may be added to the calendar, "that he and his kingdom may enjoy his suffrages and merit his patronage in heaven, who had the benefit of his conversation on earth." Nos attendentes, per Dei gratiam, fideles in Christo, nosque praecipue, et populum regni nostri, ejus posse suffragiis adjuvari, ut, quem familiarem habuimus in terris, mereamur habere patronum in caelis. Foedera, vol. i., p. 976. Edit. 1816. <div eID="gen51715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51716" type="x-p"/> Having their conscience seared with a hot iron - They bear the marks of their hypocrisy as evidently and as indelibly in their conscience in the sight of God, as those who have been cauterized for their crimes do in their bodies in the sight of men. It was customary in ancient times to mark those with a hot iron who had been guilty of great crimes, such as sacrilege, etc. And the heathens supposed that even in the other world they bear such marks; and by these the infernal judges knew the quantum of their vices, and appointed the degrees of their punishment. There is a saying much like that of the apostle in the invective of Claudian against Rufinus, whom he supposes to be thus addressed by Rhadamanthus, one of the infernal judges: - <div eID="gen51716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51717" type="x-p"/> Quid demens manifesta negas? En pectus InUstae <div eID="gen51717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51718" type="x-p"/> Deformant Maculae! vitiisque inolevit imago, <div eID="gen51718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51719" type="x-p"/> Nec sese commissa tegunt. "Thou fool, why dost thou deny what is so manifest? Behold the deep-burnt marks deform thy conscience; the appearance of them has grown up with thy vices; neither can the crimes which thou hast committed hide themselves."
entries.6536add845b099aba42b9921ee1a449f3c83965c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen51719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51720" type="x-p"/> Forbidding to marry - These hypocritical priests pretending that a single life was much more favorable to devotion, and to the perfection of the Christian life. This sentiment was held by the Essenes, a religious sect among the Jews; and we know that it is a favourite opinion among the Romanists, who oblige all their clergy to live a single life by a vow of continency. <div eID="gen51720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51721" type="x-p"/> To abstain from meats - Both among the heathens, Jews, and Romanists, certain meats were prohibited; Some always, others at particular times. This the apostle informs us was directly contrary to the original design of God; and says that those who know the truth, know this.
entries.c9f39012e57ce58848ade0fa752acfe88120c402: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen51721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51722" type="x-p"/> For every creature of God is good - That is: Every creature which God has made for man's nourishment is good for that purpose, and to be thankfully received whenever necessary for the support of human life; and nothing of that sort is at any time to be refused, ουδεν αποβλητον, rejected or despised. We find a saying very similar to this in Lucian's Timon: Ουτοι αποβλητα εισι δωρα τα παρα Διος. The gifts which are from Jove ought not to be Despised. This appears to have been a proverbial saying among the heathens.
entries.debc2df2c204341b804b2771c5b978bdd5f21c50: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen51722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51723" type="x-p"/> For it is sanctified by the word of God - Δια λογου Θεου· By the command of God; probably referring to <reference osisRef="Gen.1.29">Gen 1:29</reference> : And God said, I have given you every herb - and every tree - to you it shall be for meat; and to <reference osisRef="Gen.9.3">Gen 9:3</reference> : Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you; even as the green herb have I given you all things; i.e. I have given you every animal that is proper for food, as I have given you every herb and fruit proper for nourishment. Therefore, all this was sanctified, set apart, and appropriated to this use by this command. And when man is about to use it, he is to sanctify or set it apart to that use by prayer to God, <div eID="gen51723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51724" type="x-p"/> 1. That it may answer the end to us for which it was designed; <div eID="gen51724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51725" type="x-p"/> 2. That we may use it with gratitude and moderation; <div eID="gen51725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51726" type="x-p"/> 3. That all the strength derived from it may be devoted to God, in filling up the duties of those situations in which his providence has placed us. <div eID="gen51726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51727" type="x-p"/> Those who thank not God for their food, and pray not for his blessing in the use of it, are unworthy even of a morsel of bread, and of the breath they breathe. Bishop Newton's opinion of this prophecy I have reserved to the end of this chapter.
entries.e018a06ee835aa577dd16528eaefb02b18fdd243: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen51727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51728" type="x-p"/> If thou put the brethren in remembrance of these things - Show the Church that, even now, there is danger of this apostasy; put them on their guard against it; for the forewarned are half armed. Schoettgen supposes from this verse that what is spoken above refers to the Jews alone; and that there is no reference here to a Church which in after ages might apostatize from, or corrupt, the true doctrine of our Lord and Savior. Bishop Newton and others are of a different opinion. See at the end of this chapter. <div eID="gen51728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51729" type="x-p"/> Nourished up in the words of faith - By acting as I command thee, thou wilt show that thou art a good minister of Jesus Christ, and that thou hast been nourished from thy youth upon the doctrines of faith. The apostle seems to allude here to Timothy's Christian education. See the preface to this epistle. <div eID="gen51729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51730" type="x-p"/> Whereunto thou hast attained - Ἡ παρηκολουθηκας· Which thou hast thoroughly understood. For the meaning of this word, see the note on <reference osisRef="Luk.1.3">Luk 1:3</reference>.
entries.172038270c68877647207630e80169947d8ba66f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen51730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51731" type="x-p"/> But refuse profane and old wives' fables - This seems to refer particularly to the Jews, whose Talmudical writings are stuffed with the most ridiculous and profane fables that ever disgraced the human intellect. It may with equal propriety be applied to the legends of the Romish Church. Let any man read the Aurea Legenda, and he will find of profane and old wives' fables what may stand, with considerable propriety, column for column with the Talmud. See Joseline's Life of St. Patrick for miracles, without rhyme or reason, abundantly more numerous and more stupendous than all the necessary ones wrought by Jesus Christ and his apostles. This is enough to persuade a man that the Spirit of God had these very corruptions and this corrupt Church particularly in view. <div eID="gen51731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51732" type="x-p"/> Exercise thyself rather unto godliness - To understand this expression it is necessary to know that the apostle alludes here to the gymnastic exercises among the Greeks, which were intended as a preparation for, their contests at the public games. They did this in order to obtain a corruptible or fading crown, i. e, a chaplet of leaves, which was the reward of those who conquered in those games; Timothy was to exercise himself unto godliness, that he might be prepared for the kingdom of heaven, and there receive a crown that fadeth not away. See the notes on <reference osisRef="1Cor.9.24">1Cor 9:24</reference>, etc.
entries.ff4bd9749610631fdc46a50ed030cc08b3760ee1: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen51732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51733" type="x-p"/> For bodily exercise profiteth little - Προς ολιγον εστιν ωφελιμος. Those gymnastic exercises, so highly esteemed among the Greeks, are but little worth; they are but of short duration; they refer only to this life, and to the applause of men: but godliness has the promise of this life, and the life to come; it is profitable for all things; and for both time and eternity. <div eID="gen51733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51734" type="x-p"/> But godliness is profitable unto all things - By godliness we are to understand every thing that the Christian religion either promises or prescribes: the life of God in the soul of man; and the glory of God as the object and end of that life. To receive the first, a man must renounce his sins, deny himself, take up his cross, and follow his Lord through evil and through good report. To obtain the latter, a man must labor to enter into that rest which remains for the people of God. <div eID="gen51734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51735" type="x-p"/> Having promise, of the life that now is - The man that fears, loves, and serves God, has God's blessing all through life. His religion saves him from all those excesses, both in action and passion, which sap the foundations of life, and render existence itself often a burden. The peace and love of God in the heart produces a serenity and calm which cause the lamp of life to burn clear, strong, and permanent. Evil and disorderly passions obscure and stifle the vital spark. Every truly religious man extracts the uttermost good out of life itself, and through the Divine blessing gets the uttermost good that is in life; and, what is better than all, acquires a full preparation here below for an eternal life of glory above. Thus godliness has the promise of, and secures the blessings of, both worlds.
entries.175f44e42917b35dbe26b5be6a20f1c98c72fa78: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen51735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51736" type="x-p"/> This is a faithful saying - The truth of this doctrine none need doubt; and every man has it in his power to put this to the proof. See on <reference osisRef="1Tim.1.15">1Tim 1:15</reference> (note).
entries.5c071b556eec6cc02c3d75b35589b91190682fc5: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen51736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51737" type="x-p"/> For therefore we both labor - This verse was necessary to explain what he had before said; and here he shows that his meaning was not that the followers of God should enjoy worldly prosperity and exemption from natural evils; for, said he, it is because we exercise ourselves to godliness that we have both labor and reproach, and we have these because we trust In the living God: but still we have mental happiness, and all that is necessary for our passage through life; for in the midst of persecutions and afflictions we have the peace of God that passeth knowledge, and have all our crosses and sufferings so sanctified to us that we consider them in the number of our blessings. <div eID="gen51737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51738" type="x-p"/> Who is the Savior of all men - Who has provided salvation for the whole human race, and has freely offered it to them in his word and by his Spirit. <div eID="gen51738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51739" type="x-p"/> Specially of those that believe - What God intends for All, he actually gives to them that believe in Christ, who died for the sins of the world, and tasted death for every man. As all have been purchased by his blood so all may believe; and consequently all may be saved. Those that perish, perish through their own fault.
entries.db67771a216dce78b9c039ecca2788ba797c8a36: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen51739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51740" type="x-p"/> These things command and teach - Let it be the sum and substance of thy preaching, that true religion is profitable for both worlds; that vice destroys both body and soul; that Christ tasted death for every man; and that he saves to the uttermost all them that believe in his name.
entries.42de23977b23c390bb75842fa46fa4d6b59c9e42: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen51740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51741" type="x-p"/> Let no man despise thy youth - Act with all the gravity and decorum which become thy situation in the Church. As thou art in the place of an elder, act as an elder. Boyish playfulness ill becomes a minister of the Gospel, whatever his age may be. Concerning Timothy's age see the conclusion of the preface to this epistle. <div eID="gen51741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51742" type="x-p"/> Be thou an example of the believers - It is natural for the flock to follow the shepherd; if he go wrong, they will go wrong also. "Himself a wanderer from the narrow way, <div eID="gen51742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51743" type="x-p"/> His silly sheep, no wonder if they stray." <div eID="gen51743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51744" type="x-p"/> Though, according to the just judgement of God, they who die in their sins have their blood on their own head; yet, if they have either gone into sin or continued in it through the watchman's fault, their blood will God require at his hand. How many have endeavored to excuse their transgressions by alleging, in vindication of their conduct, "Our minister does so, and he is more wise and learned than we." What an awful account must such have to give to the Head of the Church when he appears! <div eID="gen51744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51745" type="x-p"/> In word - Εν λογῳ· In doctrine; teach nothing but the truth of God, because nothing but that will save souls. <div eID="gen51745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51746" type="x-p"/> In conversation - Εν αναστροφῃ· In the whole of thy conduct in every department which thou fillest in all thy domestic as well as public relations, behave thyself well. <div eID="gen51746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51747" type="x-p"/> In charity - Εν αγαπῃ· In love to God and man; show that this is the principle and motive of all thy conduct. <div eID="gen51747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51748" type="x-p"/> In spirit - Εν πνευματι· In the manner and disposition in which thou dost all things. How often is a holy or charitable work done in an unholy, uncharitable, and peevish spirit! To the doer, such work is unfruitful. <div eID="gen51748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51749" type="x-p"/> These words are wanting in ACDFG, and several others; both the Syriac, Erpen's Arabic, Ethiopic, Armenian, Vulgate, and Itala, and many of the fathers. Griesbach leaves them out of the text. They have in all probability been added by a later hand. <div eID="gen51749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen51750" type="x-p"/> In faith - Εν πιστει· This word πιστις is probably taken here for fidelity, a sense which it often bears in the New Testament. It cannot mean doctrine, for that has been referred to before. Be faithful to thy trust, to thy flock, to thy domestics, to the public, to thy God. Fidelity consists in honestly keeping, preserving, and delivering up when required, whatever is intrusted to our care; as also in improving whatever is delivered in trust for that purpose.
